review.focus: When conducting a direct attack on the king, ensure every attacking piece is defended or forces an immediate reply, rather than rushing with moves like 22.Rh4.

Instead, you lunged with 12...Nd4, but it collapsed under White's strike 13.Qxe5, attacking your pinned knight on f6. You entered a messy sequence of trades with 13...Nxf3 14.gxf3 Bxf3 15.Bxf6 Bxh1, but White emerged with an extra piece after 16.Bxh8, leaving your king stranded in the center.

review.focus: Calculate defensive liabilities before launching central attacks; on 12...Nd4, checking your loose pieces on e5 and f6 would have prompted a safer approach like 12...d4.

review.headline: A smooth Sicilian clamp capped by a decisive knight fork

sections.text: You handled the opening cleanly against an offbeat Sicilian setup. Black gave up their dark-squared bishop early with 7...Bxd4 8.Bxd4, and after 9.Qxd4 Nf6 10.e5, you pushed their knight right back to g8. You built an active center and developed with 11.Nc3 and 12.Bd3, leaving Black cramped and lagging in development.

Your only slip came with 13.Qd6??, trying to pin the d7-pawn against the queen on d8 (13.Qd6). The queen stepped into traffic too early, letting Black catch up in development with 13...Ne7. Instead, trading bishops with 13.Be4 would have pinned the b7-bishop against the a8-rook and maintained total control. Still, you reorganized well around the d6 outpost with 15.Nc5 and 18.Rad1.

Black cracked under the pressure on d7 and played 18...Qb6??, creating a self-pin on their c6-bishop against your queen. You punished it instantly with 19.Nxd7!, executing a fork against Black's queen on b6 and rook on f8. When Black tried 19...Rfd8?, you unleashed 20.Nxb6!, winning the queen via a discovered attack on d8, and Black resigned right after 21.Nxa8.

review.turning_point: 18...Qb6?? walked directly into your tactics, allowing 19.Nxd7! to fork queen and rook and force a winning material gain.
review.focus: Avoid prematurely anchoring your queen in enemy territory when simpler piece trades retain your bind, as seen on 13.Qd6.

review.focus: When you already have a decisive material advantage, avoid unnecessarily complex combinations like 19...Nb3+ that surrender your extra pieces.

review.focus: Remember basic opening retreats in the Rossolimo: after 4...a6, trade with 5.Bxc6 rather than retreating into 5.Ba4?? where the bishop gets trapped by ...b5.

Black allowed you back into striking distance with 13...Bd6, and you jumped on it with 14.Ng5+! driving their king up the board. However, you immediately gave up the initiative with 15.Nf3??, retreating when you needed to keep the pressure on with moves like 15.Rg1. Black pushed 15...f4, gaining space and leaving your king stranded in the center after 17.Kd1.

After 18...Nd7, you had another chance to contest the files, but 19.Nh4?? sidelined your knight and allowed Black to seize the g-file with 19...Rhg8. Black's attack broke through quickly. By move 24, trades favored Black, and 26...Nh4 cemented the pin on your f3-knight before Black finished off the game with 27...Qxe8+.

review.turning_point: The decision to sacrifice multiple minor pieces with 7.Nxf7 followed by 9.Bxe6+ left you down heavy material before completing development, making your own king vulnerable once the attack stalled.
review.focus: Avoid speculative piece sacrifices when you lag behind in development, such as 7.Nxf7, and focus on finishing development with moves like 7.N5f3.

review.headline: A passive setup crumbled under White's kingside pawn storm

sections.text: Facing the Vienna Game, your opening development was a bit cramped. After 3.f4, retreating into 3...Nd7 allowed White to seize the center with 4.fxe5 Nxe5 and 6.d4. Instead of challenging White's central space, your knights were pushed backward, giving White a free hand to develop comfortably.

White started rolling pawns on the kingside with 9.h3 and 10.g4. Here, passive defense was dangerous; playing 10...a6 was a missed opportunity to strike at the center with 10...d5. With your king still uncastled, White completed queenside castling with 11.O-O-O and opened up the center with 12.e5.

Under pressure in the center, you lashed out with 12...Nxg4, sacrificing a piece for two pawns. White accepted with 13.hxg4 Bxg4, leaving you down a piece. White then activated their bishop with 14.Bh3, and after 17.Qxf3, your queen stepped into 17...Qd7, allowing 18.Bxd7+ which lost your queen and forced your resignation.

review.turning_point: The sacrifice 12...Nxg4 cost you a piece without enough compensation, handing White complete control of the game when 12...Nd5 was necessary.
review.focus: When your opponent begins expanding on the wing with moves like 10.g4, look to counterattack in the center rather than playing quiet pawn moves like 10...a6.

review.headline: A symmetrical Petrov endgame turns into a sudden mating net

sections.text: You chose Petrov's Defense, and after early queen trades with 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7, you reached a calm, equal endgame. On move 10, you used a pin along the long diagonal with 10...Bxc3+ to double White's c-pawns. You followed up by methodically swapping minor pieces, leaving White with shattered kingside pawns after 14...Nxf3+ 15.Bxf3 Bxf3 16.gxf3.

White became reckless with their king in the single-rook ending, marching forward into your territory with 20.Kg3 and 22.Kg4. When White played 23.d4?, you had an immediate path to take over the seventh rank with 23...Re2, but you went for 23...f5+ instead. Even so, White's king was running out of safe squares.
White's king stepped directly into disaster with 25.Kg4?? instead of retreating safely to g2. You didn't hesitate, delivering a crisp mate on the spot with 25...h5#!

review.turning_point: White walked into a fatal mating net with 25.Kg4??, letting you end the game immediately with 25...h5#.
review.focus: Look for active rook infiltration in endgames rather than automatic checks; 23...Re2 would have dominated White's second rank instead of 23...f5+.

review.headline: A quick Philidor counterattack punishes an unsound sacrifice

sections.text: You chose the Philidor Defense and looked for active piece play early on, pinning the knight on f3 with 3...Bg4. After White pushed your bishop back with 6.h3, you maintained the pin with 6...Bh5. White aggressively expanded on the kingside with 7.g4 Bg6 and then jumped in with 8.Ng5?. You reacted immediately with the central break 8...d5?, though 8...h5 would have undermined White's overextended pawns cleanly.

White won a pawn with 9.exd5, but soon lost the thread. Instead of securing their advantage, White played 10.d6??, letting you develop actively with 10...Bxd6!. Then came the real gift: White went for 11.Nxf7??, hoping for a fork against your queen and rook on h8, but you simply answered with 11...Bxf7!, trading down and leaving you up a full piece after 12.Bxf7+ Kxf7.

From there, your execution was crisp. You safely tucked your king away with 14...Rf8 and 15...Kg8 before centralizing your queen with 16...Qd5. White's backward knight move 16.Nb1 opened the floodgates. You used your active knights to set up a lethal attack with 17...Nf3+ and 18...Qc6, ultimately sealing the game with 19...Nh4+ followed by 20...Qg2#.

review.turning_point: White's miscalculated sacrifice 11.Nxf7?? completely collapsed their position, handing you an extra piece and an easy path to victory after 11...Bxf7!.
review.focus: When your opponent overextends on the flank as White did with g4, look for wing counter-punches like 8...h5 rather than rushing with 8...d5?.

review.headline: A sharp kingside trap flips the game completely

sections.text: Out of the Petrov's Defense, your 3...Bc5 allowed tactical tricks that your opponent didn't immediately punish with 4.Nxe5. After White gave up a bishop with 8.Bxf7+ Rxf7 9.dxc5 Nc6, a sharp battle emerged on the kingside. You expanded with 10...h6 and 11...g5, but 12...Nh5 walked into a discovered attack on the f-file from your rook, letting White break open the center with 13.Nxe5.

White immediately threw away the advantage with 14.Qxh5, failing to see the pin on the g5-pawn. You pounced with 14...Bg4!, driving the queen into a corner. After 15.Qxh6 Rh7 16.Qxg5+ Qxg5, you had won White's queen for a rook and took full control of the attack.

You finished the game with pure aggression. With 17...Bxh3, you launched a discovered attack against the g3-bishop. After 18.gxh3 Rxh3 19.cxd6, your 19...Rxg3+ ripped open White's shelter. White was helpless against 20...Qxg3+ 21.Kf1 Nd3, leading straight to a forced win before White resigned.

review.turning_point: White's greedy 14.Qxh5 allowed 14...Bg4!, trapping the queen on the kingside and immediately swinging the game decisively in your favor.
review.focus: Tighten up your opening knowledge against 3.Bc4 in the Petrov—play 3...Nxe4 instead of 3...Bc5 to avoid giving White easy tactical chances.

review.headline: A winning queen endgame slip into a clock-induced draw

sections.text: The game grew tense right out of the opening. After routine development, 7.Qd3?? was a serious blunder, but your opponent let you off the hook with 7...Qb6??. Castling queenside gave your king shelter, and 11.Nb3 unleashed a discovered attack against Black's bishop on c5, preserving an edge into the middlegame.

Black targeted your knight on d4 with 18...Rcd8, establishing a pin along the d-file. You handled it cleanly with 19.Qb5!, forcing trades that favored you. After 20.Nxe6 and 22.Bc4, you emerged a pawn up following 24.Bxe6+ and traded down into a winning major-piece endgame.

Your passed pawn decided the race on the flank. You pushed it through with 39.a8=Q, and after trading Black's final rook on 48.Qxg2, you were entirely winning with an extra queen. You methodically drove Black's king back, but your clock expired after 64...Kh7.

review.turning_point: 19.Qb5! broke Black's pin on the d-file, trading down into a completely winning endgame.
review.focus: Practice blitz clock management so you can smoothly convert decisive advantages, such as the position after 48.Qxg2.

review.headline: A queenless middlegame scramble turns into a devastating rook mating net

sections.text: After an early queen trade with 4...Qe7, creating a pin along the e-file against your king on e8, you settled into a balanced endgame-like structure. You steadily mobilized your pieces with 8...Re8 and 11...Rad8, grabbing space in the center.

Things got tactical when White played 16.Ne5. You answered with 16...Bd6, setting up a pin on the knight against the rook on h2, but missed the cleaner capture 16...Nxe5. After 18.Rg2, 18...Be5 was another misstep where taking on d2 first was much stronger. Still, you regrouped and liquidated into a favorable rook endgame with 23...Na4+ 24.bxa4 Rxd2.

Once your rooks doubled, White's king was in deep trouble. You capitalized on 26.Rgg1 by snapping off pawns with 26...Rxf2 and 28...Rfxc2. White's king was completely cut off, allowing you to force checkmate with 29...a5+ and 30...R5c3#.

review.turning_point: White stepped onto the g-file with 26.Rgg1, allowing 26...Rxf2 to activate your rooks and coordinate an unstoppable mating net.
review.focus: Look for simple tactical captures before making quiet moves, as seen on 16...Bd6 where 16...Nxe5 was immediately winning.

sections.text: Facing the Accelerated London System, you aimed to challenge White's setup early with 2...Nc6 and 3...f6, preparing to seize space in the center. White forced open the kingside with 6.Bxg6+ hxg6 7.Qxh8, capturing your rook. You picked up the bishop with 7...exf4, but White's queen remained a dangerous intruder after 8.Qxg8.

In a messy position, 8...fxe3? allowed White to keep the initiative and grab another vital pawn. Playing 8...Ne7 9.Qh8 would have attacked the queen and defended your g6-pawn, keeping you in the fight. Instead, after 9.Qxg6+ Ke7 10.fxe3, your king was stranded in the center and down too much material.

review.turning_point: The decisive break happened with 4...e5?!, which invited 5.Qh5+ and completely shattered your kingside structure.
review.focus: Take care with early pawn pushes like 3...f6 and 4...e5?! that open lines to your uncastled king before you have completed your development.

After 24...Bxd3 and the subsequent rook trades, the game transitioned into a completely equal major-piece endgame and eventually a level rook ending.

sections.text: Out of the Bishop's Opening, you castled into safety before taking an unwarranted risk with 8...Nxe4. Grabbing that extra pawn proved risky because your queenside pieces, especially the knight on b8 and rook on a8, remained completely undeveloped while White activated their rooks.

White brought pieces forward with 20.Ng5 and 21.Ne6. Even though 21...Qxf2+ snagged another pawn, your king was running out of defenders. review.focus: Develop your undeveloped queenside pieces rather than grabbing distant pawns, as seen when 18...Qxa2 left your rook and knight stranded.

review.headline: A loose opening leads to a fatal queen loss

sections.text: The game opened quietly against Black's queenside fianchetto, but problems began when you let your knight drift forward with 9.Ne5?? and retreated awkwardly with 10.Nc4?. This allowed Black active piece play against your king.

You stepped into direct trouble with 12.Qf3?!, setting up a pin on f7. Black answered with 12...f5, and your 13.exf5? allowed a discovered attack by the bishop on b7 that captured your queen with 13...Bxf3.

review.turning_point: The game was decided on 13.exf5?, which walked into the discovered attack 13...Bxf3, losing your queen for insufficient compensation.
review.focus: Watch long diagonal alignments to your queen before opening lines, especially when playing moves like 13.exf5.

review.headline: A sharp early queen trade turned into tactical chaos where Black came out on top

sections.text: The game kicked off with an early queen exchange on move 5, entering an equal endgame-like middlegame. You castled queenside and kept solid piece harmony until White slipped with 14.Nb4??, hanging the g2-pawn. You snatched it immediately with 14...Bxg2!, winning material and opening up White's kingside.

After 15.Rg1, things got wild. Your move 15...Rd4?? set up a pin on the d3-pawn against the d2-knight, but it gave White a chance to simply play 16.Rxg2. White missed this and chased your rook with 16.c3?? instead. You found 16...Rg4!, pinning the g2-bishop to the g1-rook. After 17.f3, your 17...Rg5?? maintained the pin along the g-file but walked into danger; luckily, White blundered back with 18.Ne4??, allowing you to reposition with 18...Rg6! and secure your bishop with the pin intact.

From there, White's position completely collapsed. You picked off another pawn with 19...Bxf3 and recaptured with 20...hxg6! after 20.Rxg6. Your heavy pieces invaded effortlessly with 21...Rxh2 and 22...Rh1+, winning a whole rook and gobbling up the queenside pawns until White resigned on move 25.

review.turning_point: White's 18.Ne4?? missed the chance to exploit your rook's placement, letting you play 18...Rg6! to stabilize your extra material and dominate the board.
review.focus: When your piece is under attack, prioritize retreating it to safety rather than complicating with risky counterattacks like 15...Rd4??.

review.headline: A solid English setup undone by a single tactical oversight

sections.text: You handled the opening cleanly against White's English setup, getting castled quickly with 4...O-O and placing your knight actively on the d4-square with 7...Nd4. After White traded on e6, recapturing with 11...fxe6 gave you control over key central squares and a completely level position.

The game took an immediate turn on move 12. Instead of maintaining your coordination with 12...Bc5, you played 12...Nh5??, which left the knight entirely unprotected. White seized the gift right away with 13.Qxh5, instantly putting you down a full minor piece.

A piece behind, you tried to create counterplay by doubling rooks on the f-file with 19...Raf8. However, White used their extra piece and advanced kingside pawns to attack your rook with 21.Bg5 and 22.h5. After 22...Be1?!, White captured on g6 with 23.hxg6, winning your queen and wrapping up the game quickly.

review.turning_point: The contest was decided on move 12 when 12...Nh5?? blundered a full knight to 13.Qxh5, shifting the evaluation from +0.2 to -4.2.
review.focus: Always verify piece safety before making an attacking lunge: 12...Nh5 jumped into enemy territory without a defender.

review.headline: A tense rook endgame turns tragic with a single king step

sections.text: The game started quietly in a Giuoco Piano. After castling and trading minor pieces in the center, you simplified into an endgame by playing 15.Bxc6, 16.Qxc6, and 17.Bxb6. Both sides locked down the kingside, which shifted all the action over to the queenside files.

You doubled your rooks on the a-file and built up pressure with 21.b4 and 22.a4. When Black played 31...Rea8, they left their a7-rook unprotected. That gave you a massive tactical opportunity: 32.axb6 would have unleashed a discovered attack along the a-file from your a2-rook onto their a7-rook. Instead, you chose 32.fxe4, and after 32...Kd7, you missed the discovered attack again with 33.a6 instead of 33.axb6.

Even after letting those tactical shots slip, you pushed through with 37.e5 and kept a balanced board. But under rook checks, king safety is everything. After 39...Re4+, stepping forward with 40.Kc5 walked right into a mating net, allowing 40...Rc4# on the spot.

review.turning_point: After battling through an equal heavy-piece endgame, 40.Kc5 walked into an instant mate instead of retreating with 40.Kd3.
review.focus: Calculate forcing pawn captures on files with aligned heavy pieces: 32.axb6 was a winning tactic that bypassed the center entirely.

review.headline: A strange opening collapses under king-side dark-square pressure

sections.text: Your opponent chose an eccentric start with 1.Nh3 and 2.Na3, allowing you to establish central control and chop off both knights with 3...Bxh3 and 4...Bxa3. While this saddled White with doubled pawns on both flanks, parting with your bishops left your king-side dark squares vulnerable once the board opened.

White activated rapidly on the half-open files. Facing pressure from 8.Rg1 and 9.Qh4, you responded with 9...g6?? to shield the g-pawn. This gave away control of key dark squares, allowing 10.Bg5 to pressure your knight on f6. Instead, stepping up with 9...Qe7 would have kept your pieces defended and avoided creating glaring weaknesses.

After losing the knight to 11.Bxf6, venturing across the board with 12...Qxa3? abandoned your king's defense just as White followed up with 13.Qh6. To stay in the game, you found the deflection 13...Qc3+!, creating a fork against e1 and f6. White answered with 14.Bxc3, winning the queen and leaving you down too much material to recover.

review.turning_point: The decisive shift came with 9...g6??, which surrendered the knight on f6 to 10.Bg5 and permanently exposed your dark squares.
review.focus: Avoid creating unnecessary pawn weaknesses around your king like 9...g6, particularly when you lack the bishop needed to defend those squares.

review.headline: A wild tactical skirmish decided by a back-rank oversight

sections.text: In the Three Knights Game, things quickly got chaotic in the center. After 5.dxc3, grabbing the pawn with 5...Nxe4? ran into 6.Qd5, creating an uncomfortable dual threat against your knight and the f7-pawn. You defended with 6...Nd6, but White let you off the hook with 7.O-O??. In that moment, you had the chance to win a piece with 7...Nxc4, but instead you played 7...O-O??, allowing White to restore balance with 8.Nxe5.

The game heated up when you played 9...Qe7??, creating a pin along the e-file against White's knight on e5. White tried to exploit this with 10.Ng6??, aiming for a discovered attack down the file and a fork of your queen on e7 and rook on f8. However, White completely forgot about their own back rank.

You punished the oversight immediately with 10...Qxe1+!, winning a full rook due to the back rank weakness. After 11.Bf1 hxg6, you followed up cleanly with 12...Ne4 and 13...Qxf2+, leaving White's position in ruins before they lost on time.

review.turning_point: White's overambitious 10.Ng6?? walked right into 10...Qxe1+!, collapsing their entire position and putting you a full rook ahead.
review.focus: Look for undefended loose pieces after opponent mistakes; on move 7...O-O, you missed the simple capture 7...Nxc4 which wins White's bishop outright.

On move 5, you pinned the f6-knight with 5.Bg5, but when Black nudged your bishop with 5...h6, you maintained the pin via 6.Bh4 rather than taking with 6.Bxf6. Still, both sides developed naturally into an even middlegame.

review.headline: A dominant piece-up attack slips away in time trouble

sections.text: Out of the Petrov's Defense, your opponent pushed early with 7.e5?, giving you 7...dxe5!, which won a pawn and unleashed a discovered attack on the white queen. A few moves later, White sacrificed unnecessarily on the kingside with 11.Nxf7?. After 11...Rxf7! 12.Bxf7+ Kxf7, White had pinned your rook along the diagonal, but you emerged with two minor pieces for a rook and quickly took control of the game.

You coordinated your pieces beautifully through the middlegame, picking off pawns with 14...Bxc2 and 25...Nxb4. When White blundered with 30.Ne6+ Nxe6 31.Rxe6 Bxe6, you were an entire rook ahead. Your kingside assault forced White's king into the corner, and winning the second rook with 39...Bxd7 left White completely lost.

With the clock running down, precision disappeared. After White queued up a new queen with 40.a7, 40...Rd3? created a pin on the f3-pawn but missed a direct mating attack starting with 40...Bxg4+. White promoted with 41.a8=Q, and after 42.Kg2, 42...Rf4?? threw away your decisive edge.

White handed you one final chance with 44.h3??, allowing the crisp 44...Ne3+! 45.Kh2 Rf2+ 46.Kg1. But low on time, you played 46...Rf3?? instead of continuing the attack. When White pinned your knight with 47.Qd2??, you answered with 47...Rf1+?? delivering a back rank check, but letting the win slip right before your time ran out.

review.turning_point: After completely outplaying White, 40...Rd3? and 42...Rf4?? let White back into the game, setting the stage for a clock defeat.
review.focus: When hunting a mating net under time pressure, keep checks forceful and direct rather than retreating, as seen on 46...Rf3.

review.headline: A Swift Punishment for Reckless Opening Play

sections.text: Your opponent chose an unorthodox setup starting with 1...a5 and quickly ran into serious trouble. After 3...Nf6, you could have pushed 4.e5 immediately to seize space, but you opted for 4.Bd3. Black then lashed out with 4...g5 and blundered with 5...Nb4, ignoring the safety of their knight on f6.

You capitalized right away with 6.exf6, winning the knight and forcing Black's position to unravel. After trading queens with 7.Qe2+ Qe7 8.Qxe7+ Kxe7, you nudged the other knight with 9.a3. Black gave up the knight on c2 with 9...Nxc2+ 10.Bxc2, leaving you a full piece ahead with total central control.

From there, you activated your rooks and brought the king hunt to a swift conclusion. After 13.Re1+ Kd6 and winning Black's rook on the a-file via 16.Rxa8, your heavy pieces dominated the board. You traded down cleanly with 21.Bxd6 cxd6 and coordinated both rooks on the eighth rank to deliver 27.Ra8#.

review.turning_point: Black's blunder 5...Nb4 allowed you to take the knight on f6 with 6.exf6, securing a decisive material advantage that you never let go.
review.focus: Look for immediate pawn pushes like 4.e5 when your opponent places a knight on f6 without pawn support, rather than playing passive developing moves like 4.Bd3.

review.headline: A central pawn grab that collapsed under heavy e-file pressure

sections.text: You handled the opening cleanly, trading off bishops with 5...Bxc4 and maintaining a solid setup. When White stumbled with 10.Nd5, you found the sharpest response in 10...Nxd5!, eliminating the centralized knight and bringing your remaining knight to a strong post on e5.

The trouble began when you went hunting for pawns before securing your king. With 12...Nxc4, you took material but left your uncastled king exposed on the open e-file. White replied with 13.Qe2, setting up a pin on your e7-bishop against your king on e8 while attacking your knight on c4.

You had a chance to regroup with 13...Ne5, but 13...f6 left your knight hanging. White captured it with 14.Qxc4, leaving you down a piece. White then piled rooks on the e-file and broke through with 19.Nxf5 and 20.Rxe7+, forcing your king out and sealing the game.

review.turning_point: 12...Nxc4 grabbed a pawn at the cost of development, and after White's 13.Qe2, your reply 13...f6 dropped the knight on c4.
review.focus: Prioritize king safety over queenside pawn grabs—on move 12, simple castling with 12...O-O would have kept your position completely solid.

review.headline: A swift punishment in the Italian Game

sections.text: You set up a textbook Classical Italian, striking the center quickly with 4.c3 and 5.d4. Black made a fatal tactical oversight immediately with 5...Nf6??, completely hanging the bishop on c5. You wasted no time and grabbed the piece with 6.dxc5!, seizing a commanding advantage on move six.

After pocketing the bishop and pushing ahead with 7.exd5, you grabbed another pawn with 8.Nxe5?!. While still completely winning, 8.Be2 was a cleaner way to safeguard your bishop before finishing development. Black tried to complicate matters, but you kept your cool, safely castling and regrouping your pieces.

With 14.b4, you forced Black to give up another piece on c5. Once your queen lined up with the bishop via 16.Qd3, Black neglected the kingside threats with 16...Rad8, allowing you to crash through with 17.Qxh7+ and deliver checkmate with 18.Bg6#.

review.turning_point: Black's blunder 5...Nf6?? allowed 6.dxc5!, handing you an extra piece and complete control of the game from the opening.
review.focus: When already ahead a full piece, prioritize piece safety and development over grabbing extra pawns, such as choosing 8.Be2 instead of 8.Nxe5?!.

sections.text: You responded to 1.e4 with Petrov's Defense, steering into a solid setup with 3...d6 and 5...Be7. After castling, you pushed for queenside space with 7...c5 and 8...a5, provoking White's 9.a4.

Your only major slip came with 10...Bxb3. Giving up the bishop ceded central control and left your minor pieces with less scope. Developing naturally with 10...Nc6 was the cleanest way to maintain a balanced position.

White gave you a way back into the game with 14.Nb5, and you found the sharp reply 14...Qc6. That allowed you to scoop the central pawn with 15...Nxe4 and reinforce your knight with 16...f5, establishing a commanding +2.3 position before your time expired.

review.turning_point: White's 14.Nb5 allowed you to strike back with 14...Qc6, winning the e4-pawn and seizing full control of the game.
review.focus: Avoid parting with your active bishop pair prematurely, as happened with 10...Bxb3.

sections.text: Your opponent chose an awkward setup with 3...Bd6, blocking their own d-pawn. You wasted no time opening the center with 4.d4. After 4...exd4, you opted for 5.Nxd4, though castling first with 5.O-O was even crisper to keep maximum pressure on Black's uncoordinated pieces.

Black spent extra tempi moving the bishop again with 6...Bc5, leaving their pieces lined up against yours. After you solidified your center with 7.Be3, Black castled into disaster with 7...O-O??, completely overlooking the tactical vulnerability of their bishop on c5.

You pounced immediately with 8.Nxc6!, unleashing a discovered attack from your bishop on e3 against Black's bishop on c5 while attacking their queen. Black had to play 8...bxc6, allowing 9.Bxc5 to cleanly win a piece.

From there, you maintained complete control. After Black tried 10...Nxe4, you simplified cleanly with 11.Nxe4 Rxe4 12.Bxf7+ Kh8 13.Qd3. With the open e-file under your command after 15.Rxe1, Black decided they had seen enough and resigned.

review.focus: Look for ways to accelerate your development before recapturing pawns, such as preferring 5.O-O over 5.Nxd4 when your opponent lags in development.
